preamble: Backing and rounding of a nasalized low vowel [ã] to a nasalized back rounded vowel while nasality is kept. The clearest case is Old Polish, where the single nasal vowel /ã/ that resulted from the 14th-century merger kept a length contrast, and in the 15th century the long member was backed and rounded to [ɒ̃~ɔ̃], the source of modern ⟨ą⟩. A parallel change raised Proto-Germanic long nasalized *ą̄ to ǭ in pre-Old English. In both languages the outcome is often an open-mid [ɔ̃], which this atlas files under õ because it has no separate open-mid nasal cell.

examples.from: Old Polish long nasal /ãː/ (< Proto-Slavic *ǫ in *zǫ̑bъ 'tooth')
examples.note: In the 15th century the short nasal was fronted to [ɛ̃] (ę) and the long one was backed to [ɒ̃~ɔ̃] (ą) and lost its length. That is why ą and ę alternate within one paradigm, as in ząb 'tooth' vs. gen. sg. zęba and nom. pl. zęby.
The long nasalized *ą̄, from *anh, was not fronted by Anglo-Frisian brightening. It was raised to ǭ and later denasalized to ō, whereas Old High German kept ā (gidāht).
